chapter: Publishing, Jelly Roll in Los Angeles and band lore
title: Bunk Johnson, King Oliver, Keppard and the Creoles who passed through California
summary: Spikes had never met Bunk Johnson, places King Oliver's visit in 1921-22, and says Freddie Keppard and other Creole musicians came around 1907-09.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: Uh, how about...uh, I read in one of these magazines that Bunk Johnson visited California in 1905...

I never met Bunk. That's Jelly Roll's particular friend. He was a trumpet player, I think, too. Bunk Johnson was. He's one of them New Orleans greats like uh...uh...what's his name? Armstrong! But he was a home boy. See? He stayed in New Orleans all the time, but everybody knew...heard about him because he was so great, you know.
I just wondered, because it said he came to California in 1905, and I just wondered if you ever heard anything about that.
1905? I wouldn't know nothin' about that.
How about King Oliver in 1917? Do you remember his coming here? Or were you...1917--were you here or were you in the Army? No, you were... That was 1918 you were in the Army.

...in the Army. But King Oliver...I mean, when King Oliver come here--yeah, I told you he made 'Someday Sweetheart.' He recorded that. And I told you that when I went East, Satchmo was playin' second trumpet. King Oliver was a trumpet player. 'Course that was
in '22. I didn't think King Oliver was out here in '17. I thought he was out here around '21 or '22. They mighta been...
Well, maybe it's wrong. I just read it, and I wondered if you were here when he was here.
I was in the Army then. Or either in Honolulu-- one or the other 'cause we were in Honolulu during the '17 in the Army, and we was drafted over there.

Keppard? Yeah, he was a trumpet player. He come here in around 1907 or '8. Freddy Keppard and Jelly Roll's brother-in-law, Johnson, bass player...they came here, and Ernest Coycault--they call him Ernest Johnson, too. He came out here. A bunch of those Creoles came out of...about a year or so apart. They was one great trombone player went up North--Pappoose or something--they had all them Creole names. They all came through here '7...1907 or '8, '9, like that, you know.
